government.note: No functioning central government existed on 1 January 2000: the state collapsed in 1991, and the south was divided among clan-based armed factions. Puntland (1998) and Somaliland (1991, tag SML) ran their own administrations. The Somali National Reconciliation Conference at Arta, Djibouti, created a 245-member Transitional National Assembly in 2000, which elected a President on 26 August 2000 (Transitional National Government). It was followed by the Transitional Federal Government and Transitional Federal Parliament (2004), and by the Federal Government and Federal Parliament (2012), whose members are chosen indirectly through clan delegates. All Presidents have been elected by these bodies; there has been no direct national election. Since 30 March 2024 a constitutional crisis has divided the Federal Government from Puntland, Jubaland and later South West State, and since 15 May 2026 the opposition has disputed the President's mandate. The 'constitution' flags are rough approximations: no constitution was in effective force in 2000, and the current provisional constitution dates from 2012 (amended in 2024 and 2026).

holders.vacant_reason: No recognised central government. Ali Mahdi Muhammad's interim presidency (from January 1991) ended on 3 January 1997, although he remained a de facto claimant until August 2000. Hussein Farrah Aidid's rival claim (from 2 August 1996) was not recognised, and he gave it up in the Cairo Declaration of December 1997.

offices.review_note: Wikipedia and Wikidata disagree on the 2003-2004 changeovers: Hassan Abshir Farah's end (8 Nov vs 8 Dec 2003), Muhammad Abdi Yusuf's start and end (8 Nov 2003 - 1 Nov 2004 vs 8 Dec 2003 - 3 Nov 2004) and Ali Mohammed Ghedi's start (1 Nov vs 23 Dec 2004). Check them against a primary source. Also confirm the date the 1990s vacancy began.

start_2000.ideology_support_note: Estimate only: the last national vote before 2000 listed by Wikipedia is the 1986 presidential election, and none was held after the state collapsed in 1991. The split reflects the 2000 political landscape. Clan-based armed factions (SNA, USC wings, SSDF, SNF) form the largest block (tribal_traditional). Regional autonomy movements (Puntland, the RRA's aim of a south-western state) count as regionalist. The sharia courts of Mogadishu and wider Islamist currents count as islamist and islamic_democrat. Somali nationalism (national_conservative), Barre-era loyalists (personalist_authoritarian), and diaspora and civil-society backing for the Arta process (technocratic) make up the rest.

claims.note: Somaliland declared independence in 1991. Somalia regards it as part of its territory and does not recognise its independence.
